notes.text: About to take, &c. — It is supposed, (tho' not expressly revealed) that Elijah flourished about twenty years, before he was translated, body and soul, to heaven, only undergoing such a change, as was necessary to qualify him for being an inhabitant in that world of Spirits. By translating him, God gave in that dark and degenerate age, a very sensible proof of another life, together with a type of the ascension of Christ, and the opening of the kingdom of heaven to all believers.

Tarry here — This he desires, either,

1. That being left alone, he might better prepare himself for his great change. Or,

2. Out of indulgence to Elisha, that he might not be overwhelmed with grief at so sad a sight. Or,

3. That he might try his love, and whet his desire to accompany him; it being highly convenient for God's honour, that there should be witnesses of so glorious a translation. To Beth-el - Which was truth, tho' not the whole truth: for he was to go a far longer journey. But he was first to go to Beth-el, as also to Jericho, to the schools of the prophets there, that he might comfort, and strengthen their hearts in God's work, and give them his dying counsels.

To view — To observe this great event, Elijah's translation to heaven, which they expected every moment: and whereof they desired to be spectators, not to satisfy their own curiosity, but that they might be witnesses of it to others.

Smote the waters — These waters of old yielded to the ark, now to the prophet's mantle; which to those that wanted the ark, was an equivalent token of God's presence. When God will take his children to himself, death is the Jordan, which they must pass through. And they find a way thro' it, a safe and comfortable way. The death of Christ has divided those waters, that the ransomed of the Lord may pass over.

A double portion — Or, rather double to what the rest of the sons of the prophets receive at thy request. He alludes to the double portion of the first-born, Deut. xxi, 17. But though Elisha desired no more, yet God gave him more than he desired or expected; and he seems to have had a greater portion of the gifts of God's Spirit, than even Elijah had.

A hard thing — A rare and singular blessing, which I cannot promise thee, which only God can give; and he gives it only when, and to whom he pleaseth. If thou seest - This sign he proposed, not without the direction of God's Spirit, that hereby he might engage him more earnestly to wait, and more fervently to pray for this mercy.

A chariot of fire — In this form the angels appeared. The souls of all the faithful, are carried by an invisible guard of angels, into the bosom of Abraham. But Elijah being to carry his body with him, this heavenly guard appeared visibly: Not in an human shape, tho' so they might have born him in their arms, but in the form of a chariot and horses, that he may ride in state, may ride in triumph, like a prince, like a conqueror. See the readiness of the angels to do the will of God, even in the meanest services for the heirs of salvation! Thus he who had burned with holy zeal for God and his honour, was now conveyed in fire into his immediate presence.

My father — So he calls him for his fatherly affection to him, and for his fatherly authority which he had over him, in which respect the scholars of the prophets are called their sons. He saw his own condition like that of a fatherless child, and laments it accordingly. The chariot, &c. - Who by thy example, and counsels, and prayers, and power with God, didst more for the defense and preservation of Israel than all their chariots and horses. The expression alludes to the form of chariots and horses which he had seen.

Which fell — God so ordering it for Elisha's comfort, and the strengthening of his faith, as a pledge, that together with Elijah's mantle, his Spirit should rest upon him. And Elijah himself was gone to a place, where he needed not the mantle, either to adorn him, or to shelter him from weather, or to wrap his face in.
The Lord — Who at Elijah's request divided these waters, and is as able to do it again.

glossa.text: *It came to pass. ((RAB. in lib. Reg., t. III.))* A whirlwind, that is, a most violent wind, etc., *as far as* The Lord was taken up, neither begetting by intercourse nor begotten.

*Let it be in.* Elias was mightily strong in the spirit of prophecy and in the working of miracles, the twofold grace, therefore, which Elisaeus knew to flourish in his master, he asked to be granted to himself. Whence it is plain that he asked not to be a disciple above his master. ((RAB.)) Having received from the Lord confidence in asking, the Church asks for the Spirit of Christ, and because she has need of the remission of sins, of which Christ had no need, and of the gift of the virtues which Christ out of his fullness bestows through the Holy Spirit, *who ascending on high, led captivity captive, gave gifts to men ((Ephes. IV))*, to those, namely, who place their hope in him. Hence it is that he says:

*If thou shalt see.* That is, if thou shalt open the eyes of faith, and shalt faithfully believe, together with the passion and the resurrection, my ascension also, thou shalt obtain the effect of thy petition.

*The mantle.* ((RAB.)) It is the Incarnation, through which he broke asunder the river of death and prepared for us a passage to life, this Elisaeus retained after the passing of Elias, because the Church kept the faith of the Incarnation after the ascension of Christ, through which she strives to pass over the waves of the present life; but as Elisaeus did not divide the waters except when the name of Elias had been invoked, so the Church cannot do any works of power except through the invocation of the name of Christ. For it is God who worketh in us both to will and to accomplish.

notes.text: Night — Which to others was a time of rest and quietness.
In holiness — God is holy and just, and true in all his works.
Afraid — And stood still, as men astonished, do.
Poured — When the Israelites passed over the sea. Arrows - Hail-stones or lightnings.
Not known — Because the water returned and covered them.

Leddest — First through the sea, and afterwards through the wilderness, with singular care and tenderness, as a shepherd doth his sheep. This psalm is a narrative of the great mercies God had bestowed upon Israel, the great sins wherewith they had provoked him, and the many tokens of his displeasure at them. Here is, The preface, ver. 1-8. The general scope of this psalm, ver. 9-11. As to the particulars, we are told, what God had done for them; how ungrateful they were for his favours; how God had justly punished them; and how graciously he had spared them, notwithstanding all their provocations, ver. 12-72. Maschil of Asaph.

glossa.text: *I cried to the Lord with my voice.* ((AUG.)) With the intention of devotion toward the Lord, seeking nothing else from him, because he is Lord, and because he is God. *My voice unto him.* The voice is for this, for the sake of which it is uttered; this he adds, lest he be thought to cry to God for anything else than for himself, above whom there is nothing. ((CAS.)) He does not say what he asks, because there is no need that it be said to him who knows what is expedient. *He hath attended to me.* ((CAS.)) *For God to attend* is to give the whole of what is asked, and more than is asked.

*In the day of my trouble I sought.* ((AUG.)) How didst thou seek? etc., *as far as* he who does not do justice before men, that he may be seen. *He refused to be comforted.* ((ID.)) He expounds the tribulation, etc., *as far as* he who in all men either finds or fears a scandal, is secure in none.

*In thy inventions.* ((AUG.)) That is, in the precepts which thou hast invented, or by which thou art found. ((CAS.)) Or *in thy observances,* that is, in the precepts which are to be observed, I shall be exercised: because it is not enough to read the Scriptures, but it behoves to show the fruit of works: instructed by these he breaks forth into praises. ((AUG.)) *In thy inventions* or *thy affections,* not in mine; or there is affection in earthly things: so in the works and in the meditation of God there is a certain inward affection, when the world is beheld, and in creatures the creator is sought, and is found nowhere displeasing, but everywhere pleasing.

*O God, in the holy place.* ((AUG.)) By the things aforesaid I am certain that I shall come, and with him for guide. ((ID.)) *O God, in the holy place,* that is, in Christ, the way of returning to thee. And since this is so, *who is a great God?* etc. *Thy way.* ((ID.)) Of worshipping thee and of coming to thee, whence he joyfully prefers the power of God to the images, which were falsely worshipped.

*Wonders.* ((AUG.)) The deaf, the blind, the feeble, the dead, the paralytic were healed. These things were done in bodies. In the soul certain men are sober, who a little before were drunkards, unbelievers, adorers of images. *To the peoples thy power.* ((ID.)) *To the unfaithful, that* they may know Christ only in body, *to the faithful,* in reality and in Godhead; he subjoins: What thou hast bestowed, *thou hast redeemed.*

*The sons of Joseph.* ((AUG.)) That is, the Gentile people. Or, by *Joseph* Christ is understood: because, as Joseph, sold into Egypt, reigned, so Christ reigned among the Gentiles, having first been humbled in the martyrs. ((ID.)) *Joseph,* who came to the Gentiles, is interpreted *increase:* and he signifies the Gentiles, from whom the people of God has been increased. Or, *Joseph,* Christ sold by the Jews, and driven to the Gentiles, *his sons,* whom he chose out of the Gentiles.

*They saw.* ((CAS.)) Diapsalma. He expounds what things Christ works in the world. ((AUG.)) As if he should say: Since thou hast made thy power known, either through him *they saw thee, O God the Father,* or, *thee, O Christ,* who art the power and the arm, etc.

*A multitude.* ((CAS.)) Not a few, but *a multitude. The noise,* in the groaning for faults, in the giving of thanks: for the divers vows of the peoples sound as it were a broken sea. *The noise of waters.* ((AUG.)) Whence are these noises of waters, this troubling of the deeps? because *the clouds have uttered a voice,* of which: *I will command my clouds that they rain no rain upon it.*

*The voice of thunder.* ((CAS.)) The voice of thunder is rolled about, so that a wrinkled and winding sound is perceived. An allegory: *in the wheel* of the whole world. *A wheel.* ((HIER., AUG.)) It is that which he expounds as the circle of the earth, which the clouds went about, thundering with precepts, flashing with miracles. *The earth trembled.* ((CAS.)) They who dwell in the earth. That very earth is called a sea by a likeness, because human life is bitter, subject to tempests, where the greater fish devours the lesser.

*In the sea.* ((AUG.)) To the letter, when Christ walked upon the waters. Or, in the hearts of men, whom he subjects to himself. Or, by *the land,* the Jews; by *the sea,* the Gentiles are understood. *And thy footsteps shall not be known.* A silent rebuke of the Jews; as if he should say: Although he came openly, and showed himself by miracles, he was not known by the unbelieving Jews whom he led forth in the hand of Moses and Aaron, that is, by the working of the miracles which they did. *Thy footsteps,* etc. He touched some, that is, the Jews, who say, Christ has not yet come; they do not see him walking upon the sea.

*As sheep.* Because they are not truly sheep, but goats. *Of Moses and Aaron.* ((CAS.)) Moses is interpreted *intrepretatur* *taken up from the river;* Aaron, *a mountain of strength:* by these names the powers which they wrought are expressed. Moses among other things made a way in the sea, signifying that the people is delivered through baptism. Aaron held the image of the Church, which is compared to a most strong mountain.

notes.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty — From the ceremonial law. Wherewith Christ hath made us - And all believers, free; and be not entangled again with the yoke of legal bondage.

Ye have been called to liberty — From sin and misery, as well as from the ceremonial law. Only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh - Take not occasion from hence to gratify corrupt nature. But by love serve one another - And hereby show that Christ has made you free.

For all the law is fulfilled in this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself — inasmuch as none can do this without loving God, 1 John iv, 12; and the love of God and man includes all perfection. Lev. xix, 18.

But if — On the contrary, in consequence of the divisions which those troublers have occasioned among you, ye bite one another by evil speaking. And devour one another - By railing and clamour. Take heed ye be not consumed one of another - By bitterness, strife, and contention, our health and strength, both of body and soul, are consumed, as well as our substance and reputation.
I say then — He now explains what he proposed, ver. 13. Walk by the Spirit - Follow his guidance in all things. And fulfil not - In anything. The desire of the flesh - Of corrupt nature.

For the flesh desireth against the Spirit — Nature desires what is quite contrary to the Spirit of God. But the Spirit against the flesh- - But the Holy Spirit on his part opposes your evil nature. These are contrary to each other - The flesh and the Spirit; there can be no agreement between them. That ye may not do the things which ye would- - That, being thus strengthened by the Spirit, ye may not fulfil the desire of the flesh, as otherwise ye would do.
But if ye are led by the Spirit — Of liberty and love, into all holiness. Ye are not under the law - Not under the curse or bondage of it; not under the guilt or the power of sin.

Now the works of the flesh — By which that inward principle is discovered. Are manifest - Plain and undeniable. Works are mentioned in the plural because they are distinct from, and often inconsistent with, each other. But "the fruit of the Spirit" is mentioned in the singular, ver. 22, as being all consistent and connected together. Which are these - He enumerates those "works of the flesh" to which the Galatians were most inclined; and those parts of "the fruit of the Spirit" of which they stood in the greatest need. Lasciviousness - The Greek word means anything inward or outward that is contrary to chastity, and yet short of actual uncleanness.

Idolatry, witchcraft — That this means witchcraft, strictly speaking, (not poisoning,) appears from its being joined with the worship of devil-gods, and not with murder. This is frequently and solemnly forbidden in the Old Testament. To deny therefore that there is, or ever was, any such thing, is, by plain consequence, to deny the authority both of the Old and New Testament. Divisions - In domestic or civil matters. Heresies are divisions in religious communities.

Revellings — Luxurious entertainments. Some of the works here mentioned are wrought principally, if not entirely, in the mind; and yet they are called "works of the flesh." Hence it is clear, the apostle does not by "the flesh" mean the body, or sensual appetites and inclinations only, but the corruption of human nature, as it spreads through all the powers of the soul, as well as all the members of the body. Of which I tell you before - Before the event, I forewarn you.

Love — The root of all the rest. Gentleness - Toward all men; ignorant and wicked men in particular. Goodness - The Greek word means all that is benign, soft, winning, tender, either in temper or behaviour.
Meekness — Holding all the affections and passions in even balance.

And they that are Christ's — True believers in him. Have thus crucified the flesh - Nailed it, as it were, to a cross whence it has no power to break loose, but is continually weaker and weaker. With its affections and desires - All its evil passions, appetites, and inclinations.

If we live by the Spirit — If we are indeed raised from the dead, and are alive to God, by the operation of his Spirit. Let us walk by the Spirit - Let us follow his guidance, in all our tempers, thoughts, words, and actions.

glossa.text: *Give not liberty.* The sense is: Beware lest, having heard the name of liberty, you think that you may sin unpunished. *But by the charity of the Spirit.* Charity is to be had not by the affection of the flesh, but by the spirit.

*For all the law.* For both those things which pertain to good morals, and those things which are in the sacraments (since they are well understood by the free, and not carnally observed by servants), must needs be referred to charity. *Thou shalt love thy neighbour.* This is written in Leviticus ((Levit. XIX)), in which he rightly says that the whole law is fulfilled, although there are two precepts of charity on which the whole law hangs, and the prophets, because the love of God is contained in the love of the neighbour; and therefore in this precept is the perfection of salvation, because without the neighbour God is not loved: *For he that loveth not his neighbour, whom he seeth, how can he love God, whom he seeth not? ((I Joan. IV.))* Since therefore each precept is such that neither can be held without the other, it suffices to mention one of them. *As thyself.* He cannot love his neighbour who does not love himself. But he does not love himself who loves iniquity. *For he that loveth iniquity hateth his own soul ((Psal. X))*.

*You devour.* Or *you accuse one another,* that is, laying crimes upon one another. *Lest you be consumed one of another.* By the schism of the Christian religion, by vain glory and vain victory, the occasion of charity being changed, he touched this vice of theirs, because dissension is the enemy of love. For by this vice most of all, of contention and of envy, pernicious quarrels also were nourished among them, by which fellowship and life are consumed.

*But I say in Christ,* etc. He shows how sufficient the faith of Christ is without the law, because through it they overcome the flesh and its works, and follow the spirit; as if he should say: Give not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but serve through the charity of the spirit. But this I say can be to you in Christ, and never otherwise. *You shall not fulfil,* etc. He does not say, You shall not do, or You shall not have, because they were not able not to have them, but, You shall not fulfil, that is, you shall not fulfil their works by the consent of the will.

*For the flesh lusteth,* etc. The flesh is said to lust, because the soul does this according to it, as the ear is said to hear, and the eye to see, whereas rather the soul both hears through the ear and sees through the eye. For the flesh lusts nothing save through the soul, but it is said to lust when the soul by carnal concupiscence struggles against the spirit. For the cause of that carnal concupiscence is not in the soul, for it comes to be out of both, because without both no delight is felt.

*But if you are led by the Spirit,* etc. From which it appears that he has not the Holy Spirit who is under the law, not by dispensation, but truly. *You are not under the law.* You have now this advantage, therefore this part is to be chosen. He says that those are damnably under the law whom the law makes guilty, not fulfilling the law while, not knowing grace, they presume upon themselves. Further, he is under the law who abstains from evil by fear, not by love, guilty in will. This law strikes fear, not love.
*The kingdom not of God shall they obtain.* There is no middle place, so that he should not be in punishment who will not be in the kingdom.

*Charity.* He has set the head first, whence the members follow. For no one rejoices well who does not love the good whence he rejoices. He has not true peace with anyone unless he love him. He is not long-suffering in waiting perseveringly unless he be fervent in loving. He is not kind unless he love him whom he helps. He is not good save by loving. He is not faithful healthfully, save by that faith which works through love. He is not meek who is not governed by love. No one holds himself back from that whereby he is defiled unless he love that whereby he is honoured. With reason therefore he so often commends charity, as though it alone were to be enjoined, which cannot be had without the rest by which a man is made good. *Joy.* Purity of conscience. Whence: *There is no rejoicing for the wicked, saith the Lord ((Isa. XLVIII))* .

*But they who.* As if he should say: Against the evil the law is set; but for the good the cross is set. Which he says thus: *But they who,* etc., *have crucified their flesh,* etc. It befits our devotion that we who celebrate the passion of the crucified Lord should make for ourselves a cross of carnal pleasures to be repressed. On this cross indeed ought always in this life to hang the Christian, that he may be fixed with nails and with the precepts of justice, as Christ was fastened with nails on the cross.

*If we live by the spirit.* What he said above in general he turns back upon those to whom he writes, and numbers himself with them, showing by this that he does not say to them what he himself would not be willing to keep. As if he should say: I do not say to you anything which I myself also am unwilling to do.

notes.text: The days are fulfilled that he should be received up — That is, the time of his passion was now at hand. St. Luke looks through this, to the glory which was to follow. He steadfastly set his face - Without fear of his enemies, or shame of the cross, Heb. xii, 2.
He sent messengers to make ready — A lodging and needful entertainment for him and those with him.
His face was as though he would go to Jerusalem — It plainly appeared, he was going to worship at the temple, and thereby, in effect, to condemn the Samaritan worship at Mount Gerizim.

As Elisha did — At or near this very place, which might put it into the minds of the apostles to make the motion now, rather than at any other time or place, where Christ had received the like affront.
Ye know not what manner of spirit — The spirit of Christianity is. It is not a spirit of wrath and vengeance, but of peace, and gentleness, and love.
Matt. viii, 19.
But Jesus said to him — First understand the terms: consider on what conditions thou art to follow me.
Suffer me first to bid them farewell that are in my house — As Elisha did after Elijah had called him from the plough, 1 Kings xix, 19; to which our Lord's answer seems to allude.
Is fit for the kingdom of God — Either to propagate or to receive it.

glossa.text:
*Lord, wilt thou. ((BED.))* The apostles, still rude and ignorant of the measure of vengeance, etc., *as far as* such a power has been conferred by God upon holy men.

*We say that fire come down from heaven.* At the word of these men fire would come down from heaven, because they are the sons of thunder. *And consume them? And turning he rebuked them and said.* In the likeness of Elias, who both by his own hand and by fire divinely obtained put the elders of Baal to death. And in this, that the apostles presume to themselves the power of such a prophet, it is shown that the merit of the prophets was in them.

((AMBR.)) The apostles do not sin, who follow the law, etc., *as far as* he does not seek vengeance who does not fear.
*You know not of what spirit you are.* By whose spirit you have been sealed, whose deeds you imitate, now taking counsel mercifully, but in the future judging justly.

*The Son of man came not to destroy souls, but to save,* etc. Perfect virtue has no zeal for vengeance, nor is there any anger where there is the fulness of charity.

((BED.)) Vengeance is not always to be taken upon those who sin, etc., *as far as* from whom in this place the fire is kept back.
*A certain man said. ((ID.))* This man, moved by the greatness of the signs, wishes to follow, etc., *as far as* and he feigned the service of a disciple, which feigning is figured by the fox.

*The foxes have holes. ((ID.))* The fox is a deceitful animal, intent upon ambushes, practising the robberies of fraud, dwelling in holes even amid the very lodgings of men: so the heretic, not having the house of faith, draws others into his own fraud and seduces them from the faith.

*And he said to another.* Note that the Lord spurned not faults but frauds, because he who rejected the fraudulent man chose the innocent one; but him whose father he knew to be dead, that father of whom it is said: *Forget thy father's house ((Psal. XLIV))*, etc.
*Suffer that the dead. ((BED.))* Mystically. The son is not called back from his duty to his father, etc., *as far as* he ought not to bury the devil's treacheries in himself.

*To take leave of those.* If a disciple about to follow God is rebuked because he wishes to take leave of his house, what will become of those who often, with no profit, visits the houses of their own people which they had forsaken.

echoes.text: I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, that you should not be their slaves. I have broken the bars of your yoke, and made you go upright.
echoes.note: Paul's 'yoke of bondage/slavery' inverts the exodus formula where God 'broke the bars of your yoke' and made Israel walk upright after Egyptian slavery. Volume is fair (the yoke-of-slavery image is distinctively exodus/covenant) and coheres with Paul's whole exodus-from-law typology in Galatians. The redemptive-liberation logic matches closely.

echoes.text: You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.
echoes.note: The Jubilee proclamation of 'liberty (deror) throughout the land' may underlie Paul's stress on the freedom for which Christ liberated. Coherence is real (release from debt-servitude) but volume is faint; the verbal link runs through the LXX language of eleutheria rather than direct citation.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: The Servant's anointing 'to proclaim liberty to the captives' is a Second-Temple touchstone for eschatological release that Paul's freedom language may draw upon. Faint volume and no verbal quotation, but the messianic-liberty theme coheres with Christ as the agent who 'made us free.'
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

echoes.text: Thus speaks Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, saying, I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's sign-act of the broken/iron yoke (chs. 27-28) gives the prophetic vocabulary of a yoke as imposed servitude that is broken or re-imposed. Coherence is moderate but recurrence is weak; the image is generic enough that direct dependence is uncertain.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Elijah answered to the captain of fifty, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from the sky, and consume you and your fifty!” Fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty. Again he sent to him another captain of fifty and his fifty. He answered him, “Man of God, the king has said, ‘Come down quickly!’” Elijah answered them, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from the sky, and consume you and your fifty!” The fire of God came down […]
echoes.note: 'Command fire to come down from the sky... just as Elijah did' explicitly cites Elijah calling down fire on the messengers from Samaria; the Samaritan setting makes the reference exact. High volume (named comparison) and coherence; Jesus' rebuke signals a deliberate contrast with the Elijah model.

echoes.text: When Yahweh was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.
echoes.note: 'The days were near that he should be taken up' and Jesus 'set his face' draw on Elijah's assumption ('when the LORD was about to take up Elijah') and prophetic resolve. The analepsis/analambano language tightly binds the journey's start to Elijah's ascent; high coherence.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.
echoes.note: Jesus 'set his face' resolutely toward Jerusalem echoes the Servant's 'I have set my face like a flint' in obedient suffering. Moderate volume via the face-setting idiom; coherent with the Isaianic Servant strand running through the chapter.

echoes.text: Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem, and preach toward the sanctuaries, and prophesy against the land of Israel;
echoes.note: 'Set your face toward Jerusalem and prophesy' is a recurring prophetic commission idiom that colors Jesus' face-setting as prophetic confrontation. The phrase is multiply attested in Ezekiel, so diffuse and contested.

echoes.text: So he departed there, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing, with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed over to him, and cast his mantle on him. He left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?” He returned from following him, and took the yoke of oxen, and killed them, […]
echoes.note: 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back' directly engages Elisha's call: found plowing, he asks to kiss his parents farewell before following, and Elijah lets him. Jesus radicalizes the precedent—no looking back, no delayed farewell—making the plowing image and the farewell request unmistakable. Very high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: He left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?”
echoes.note: 'Allow me first to say good-bye to those at my house' nearly quotes Elisha's 'let me kiss my father and mother, and then I will follow you.' The verbal correspondence in the third would-be follower is the strongest single anchor for the Elisha typology here.

echoes.text: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”
echoes.note: 'Looking back' as fatal hesitation may glance at Lot's wife, the proverbial backward look that forfeits deliverance. Faint and figural relative to the dominant Elisha frame; contested.

echoes.text: And he called him, and said, “My child, if I die, bury me. Don’t despise your mother. Honor her all the days of your life, and do that which is pleasing to her, and don’t grieve her.
echoes.note: 'Let me first bury my father' reflects the supreme filial duty of burial dramatized in Tobit, against which Jesus' 'leave the dead to bury their dead' is shockingly subversive. Deuterocanonical availability illuminates the cultural weight Jesus overturns, though it is background rather than a textual echo.

echoes.text: but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him into the ship, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship.
echoes.note: 'The birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head' may faintly invert creation's provision of resting places (the dove finding no rest, then nesting). Very low volume; offered only as a faint figural counterpoint.

notes.text: The son, &c. — That is, his grand-son, for he was the son of Jehosaphat, 2 Kings ix, 2. This was intended as a prediction that by these God would punish the degenerate Israelites, plead his own cause among them, and avenge the quarrel of his covenant.

Was plowing — Who had twelve ploughs going, whereof eleven were managed by his servants, and the last by himself; according to the simplicity of those ancient times, in which men of good estate submitted to the meanest employments. Cast his mantle - By that ceremony conferring upon him the office of a prophet, which God was pleased to accompany with the gifts and graces of his spirit.

He ran — Being powerfully moved by God's spirit to follow Elijah, and wholly give up himself to his function. Let me kiss - That is, bid them farewell. Go - And take thy leave of them, and then return to me again. For what, &c. - Either first, to hinder thee from performing that office. That employment to which I have called thee, doth not require an alienation of thy heart from thy parents, nor the total neglect of them. Or, secondly, to make such a change in thee, that thou shouldst be willing to forsake thy parents, and lands, and all, that thou mayest follow me. Whence comes this marvelous change? It is not from me, who did only throw my mantle over thee; but from an higher power, even from God's spirit, which both changed thy heart, and consecrated thee to thy prophetical office: which therefore it concerns thee vigourously to execute, and wholly to devote thyself to it.

From him — From Elijah to his parents; whom when he had seen and kissed, he returned to Elijah. The instruments - That is, with the wood belonging to the plow, &c. to which more was added, as occasion required. But that he burned, to shew his total relinquishing of his former employment. And gave - That is, he made thereof a feast for his servants who had been ploughing with him, and for him, and his other friends and neighbours who came to take their leave of him. Hereby he shewed how willingly and joyfully he forsook all his friends, that he might serve God in that high and honourable employment. It is of great advantage to young ministers, to spend some time under the direction of those that are aged and experienced; and not to think much, if occasion be, to minister unto them. Those who would be fit to teach, must have time to learn; those should first serve, who may hereafter rule. Ben-hadad's invasion of Israel and insolent demand, ver. 1- 12. Ahab, encouraged by a prophet, overthrows him twice, ver. 13-30. Makes a covenant with him, ver. 31-34. Is reproved and threatened by a prophet, ver. 35-43.

glossa.text:
*He departed.* When our Redeemer, coming down from heaven, by the divine judgment acquired a people still gaping after earthly works, in whom he wrought salvation, when he converted him to the faith. For Elias is interpreted the Lord God, Saphat judging, Eliseus the salvation of my God. Upon whom the prophet cast his mantle, when the Lord clothed the people with the catholic faith. Whence the Apostle: *You who are baptized in Christ, have put on Christ ((Gal. III))*. Leaving the oxen he ran after Elias: because the choir of the elect, having heard, *unless a man renounce all things, he cannot be my disciple ((Luc. XIV))*, straightway ceased to gape after earthly gains, to serve secular desires, and so preached the word of life to others, for this is to kiss father and mother, to will to correct by speech whomsoever one can, whether of the Jews or of the Gentiles.

((RAB.)) The Christian people also, slaying carnal desires, turns its whole army into the work of evangelizing, whence it may be able to furnish sufficient food to its helpers.
*He followed.* ((ID.)) He follows our Elias and ministers to him who, following his footsteps, that is, keeping his commandments, busies himself to render worthily ministry and honour.

notes.text: To thee — Thou dost not need me or my service, nor art capable of any advantage from it.

But — I bear a singular respect and love to all saints, for thy sake, whose friends and servants they are, and whose image they bear. This more properly agrees to David, than to Christ, whose goodness was principally designed for, and imparted to sinners.

Sorrows — Having shewed his affection to the servants of the true God, he now declares what an abhorrency he has for those that worship idols. Offerings - In which the Gentiles used sometimes to drink part of the blood of their sacrifices. Names - Of those other gods mentioned before.

The Lord — I rejoice in God as my portion, and desire no better, no other felicity. Cup - The portion which is put into my cup, as the ancient manner was in feasts, where each had his portion of meat, and of wine allotted to him. Lot - My inheritance divided to me by lot, as the custom then was.
Lines — My portion, which was measured with lines. Are fallen - In a land flowing with milk and honey, and above all, blessed with the presence and knowledge of God.

The Lord — Hath inspired that wisdom into me, by which I have chosen the Lord for my portion, and am so fully satisfied with him. Reins - My inward thoughts and affections, being inspired and moved by the Holy Spirit. Instruct - Direct me how to please God, and put my whole trust in him. Night - Even when others are asleep, my mind is working upon God, and improving the silence and solitude of holy meditations.

I have set — I have always presented him to my mind, as my witness and judge, as my patron and protector. Hitherto David seems to have spoken with respect to himself, but now he is transported by the spirit of prophecy, and carried above himself, to speak as a type of Christ, in whom this and the following verses were truly accomplished. Christ as man did always set his father's will and glory before him. Right-hand - To strengthen, protect, assist, and comfort me: as this assistance of God was necessary to Christ as man. Moved - Though the archers shoot grievously at me, and both men and devils seek my destruction, and God sets himself against me as an enemy, yet I am assured he will deliver me out of all my distresses.

My glory — My tongue, which is a man's glory and privilege, above all other living creatures. Rejoiceth - Declares my inward joy. For this word signifies not so much eternal joy, as the outward demonstrations of it. My flesh - My body shall quietly rest in the grave. Shall rest - in confident assurance of its incorruption there, and of its resurrection to an immortal life: the flesh or body is in itself, but a dead lump of clay; yet hope is here ascribed to it figuratively, as it is to the brute creatures, Rom. viii, 19.

Hell — In the state of the dead. Holy one - Me thy holy son, whom thou hast sanctified and sent into the world. It is peculiar to Christ, to be called the holy one of God. To see - To be corrupted or putrefied in the grave, as the bodies of others are.

Life — Thou wilt raise me from the grave, and conduct me to the place and state of everlasting felicity. Presence - In that heavenly paradise, where thou art gloriously present, where thou dost clearly and fully discover the light of thy countenance; whereas in this life thou hidest thy face and shewest us only thy back-parts. Right-hand - Which he mentions as a place of the greatest honour, the place where the saints are placed at the last day, and where Christ himself is said to sit, chap. cx, 1. Pleasures - All our joys are empty and defective: But in heaven there is fulness of joy. Our pleasures here are transient and momentary; but those at God's right hand are pleasures forevermore. For they are the pleasures of immortal souls, in the enjoyment of an eternal God. David appealing to God for his integrity, begs for defense against his enemies, ver. 1-9. Describes their wickedness, ver. 10- 12. Prays for deliverance from them, and rests in hope, ver. 13-15. A prayer of David.

glossa.text: *The inscription of a title.* ((CASS.)) This title is taken from the Gospel, not from the Old Testament. What the title noted, that is, victory and kingdom, belongs to Christ, and that is what is treated of here.

*Preserve me,* etc. The second psalm, which touches briefly on the passion and the resurrection; first, Christ, showing the one nature of man, asks to be preserved, saying that all that he endured has been brought through to the glory of his inheritance. ((AUG.)) Christ speaks here according to his manhood, of whom the royal title stood out in the passion: *Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.--Of my goods,* etc. ((CASS.)) If God has no need of the goods of Christ the man, but Christ the man has all things from him, the arrogance of men is overthrown, and the heresy of the Pelagians, who think that anything is done by their own good powers.

*To the saints who are in the land. ((Ibid.))* Christ has now set out how he prayed; he now tells what good things God did for him. ((AUG.)) *To the saints,* etc., *as far as* and power that I might rise again.

*He hath made wonderful.* ((CASS.)) As if to say, these things I said to the Lord: but the Lord made them wonderful, that is, he made my wills wonderful; and they are wonderful in that those who obey them become heavenly out of earthly.
*They are multiplied. ((Ibid.))* Whereby he made them wonderful, etc., *as far as* which sound together in one note, by which his wills are shown.

*The portion of my inheritance.* ((AUG.)) Let others choose other things, etc., *as far as* but those who choose God as their portion. ((CASS.)) Or, *the Lord* is the *portion,* that is, the share and the reward, *of my inheritance,* that is, of the saints. And *the portion of my cup,* that is, the wage of the passion. For the inheritance belongs to the Gentiles, the cup to the passion, which when drunk gives resurrection. But let no one think himself an heir save he that is illustrious.

*The lines,* etc. ((Ibid.)) As it were by lot, in which is the divine election, as the lot also fell upon Matthias, and each man takes according to his own measure. *In goodly places.* That is, among the saints.

*I will bless the Lord. ((Ibid.))* He gives thanks to the Father for understanding, and for the passion, in which by his favour he conquers, and for the resurrection, and for confession; and these are the things through which the inheritance is restored, so that he is king of the Jews, as the title says. *Understanding,* etc. ((AUG.)) Whereby this inheritance can be seen and possessed. *Moreover,* etc. That is, above understanding. *Even till night,* etc. That is, till death, he hath instructed me, that is, my lower part, the assumption of flesh, that he might drive out the darknesses of mortality which that understanding does not have, because for them it could neither be troubled nor fail. *My reins.* From whom according to the flesh I came forth, namely my kindred: they have chided me with injuries, with temptation and with passion.
*I set the Lord before me. ((Ibid.))* From this draw an example, whereby sins may be shunned: for he who always beholds God with the keen edge of the mind is not bowed down by sins.

notes.text: Stand fast therefore in the liberty — From the ceremonial law. Wherewith Christ hath made us - And all believers, free; and be not entangled again with the yoke of legal bondage.

Ye have been called to liberty — From sin and misery, as well as from the ceremonial law. Only use not liberty for an occasion to the flesh - Take not occasion from hence to gratify corrupt nature. But by love serve one another - And hereby show that Christ has made you free.

For all the law is fulfilled in this, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself — inasmuch as none can do this without loving God, 1 John iv, 12; and the love of God and man includes all perfection. Lev. xix, 18.

But if — On the contrary, in consequence of the divisions which those troublers have occasioned among you, ye bite one another by evil speaking. And devour one another - By railing and clamour. Take heed ye be not consumed one of another - By bitterness, strife, and contention, our health and strength, both of body and soul, are consumed, as well as our substance and reputation.
I say then — He now explains what he proposed, ver. 13. Walk by the Spirit - Follow his guidance in all things. And fulfil not - In anything. The desire of the flesh - Of corrupt nature.

For the flesh desireth against the Spirit — Nature desires what is quite contrary to the Spirit of God. But the Spirit against the flesh- - But the Holy Spirit on his part opposes your evil nature. These are contrary to each other - The flesh and the Spirit; there can be no agreement between them. That ye may not do the things which ye would- - That, being thus strengthened by the Spirit, ye may not fulfil the desire of the flesh, as otherwise ye would do.
But if ye are led by the Spirit — Of liberty and love, into all holiness. Ye are not under the law - Not under the curse or bondage of it; not under the guilt or the power of sin.

Now the works of the flesh — By which that inward principle is discovered. Are manifest - Plain and undeniable. Works are mentioned in the plural because they are distinct from, and often inconsistent with, each other. But "the fruit of the Spirit" is mentioned in the singular, ver. 22, as being all consistent and connected together. Which are these - He enumerates those "works of the flesh" to which the Galatians were most inclined; and those parts of "the fruit of the Spirit" of which they stood in the greatest need. Lasciviousness - The Greek word means anything inward or outward that is contrary to chastity, and yet short of actual uncleanness.

Idolatry, witchcraft — That this means witchcraft, strictly speaking, (not poisoning,) appears from its being joined with the worship of devil-gods, and not with murder. This is frequently and solemnly forbidden in the Old Testament. To deny therefore that there is, or ever was, any such thing, is, by plain consequence, to deny the authority both of the Old and New Testament. Divisions - In domestic or civil matters. Heresies are divisions in religious communities.

Revellings — Luxurious entertainments. Some of the works here mentioned are wrought principally, if not entirely, in the mind; and yet they are called "works of the flesh." Hence it is clear, the apostle does not by "the flesh" mean the body, or sensual appetites and inclinations only, but the corruption of human nature, as it spreads through all the powers of the soul, as well as all the members of the body. Of which I tell you before - Before the event, I forewarn you.

Love — The root of all the rest. Gentleness - Toward all men; ignorant and wicked men in particular. Goodness - The Greek word means all that is benign, soft, winning, tender, either in temper or behaviour.
Meekness — Holding all the affections and passions in even balance.

And they that are Christ's — True believers in him. Have thus crucified the flesh - Nailed it, as it were, to a cross whence it has no power to break loose, but is continually weaker and weaker. With its affections and desires - All its evil passions, appetites, and inclinations.

If we live by the Spirit — If we are indeed raised from the dead, and are alive to God, by the operation of his Spirit. Let us walk by the Spirit - Let us follow his guidance, in all our tempers, thoughts, words, and actions.

glossa.text: *Give not liberty.* The sense is: Beware lest, having heard the name of liberty, you think that you may sin unpunished. *But by the charity of the Spirit.* Charity is to be had not by the affection of the flesh, but by the spirit.

*For all the law.* For both those things which pertain to good morals, and those things which are in the sacraments (since they are well understood by the free, and not carnally observed by servants), must needs be referred to charity. *Thou shalt love thy neighbour.* This is written in Leviticus ((Levit. XIX)), in which he rightly says that the whole law is fulfilled, although there are two precepts of charity on which the whole law hangs, and the prophets, because the love of God is contained in the love of the neighbour; and therefore in this precept is the perfection of salvation, because without the neighbour God is not loved: *For he that loveth not his neighbour, whom he seeth, how can he love God, whom he seeth not? ((I Joan. IV.))* Since therefore each precept is such that neither can be held without the other, it suffices to mention one of them. *As thyself.* He cannot love his neighbour who does not love himself. But he does not love himself who loves iniquity. *For he that loveth iniquity hateth his own soul ((Psal. X))*.

*You devour.* Or *you accuse one another,* that is, laying crimes upon one another. *Lest you be consumed one of another.* By the schism of the Christian religion, by vain glory and vain victory, the occasion of charity being changed, he touched this vice of theirs, because dissension is the enemy of love. For by this vice most of all, of contention and of envy, pernicious quarrels also were nourished among them, by which fellowship and life are consumed.

*But I say in Christ,* etc. He shows how sufficient the faith of Christ is without the law, because through it they overcome the flesh and its works, and follow the spirit; as if he should say: Give not liberty for an occasion to the flesh, but serve through the charity of the spirit. But this I say can be to you in Christ, and never otherwise. *You shall not fulfil,* etc. He does not say, You shall not do, or You shall not have, because they were not able not to have them, but, You shall not fulfil, that is, you shall not fulfil their works by the consent of the will.

*For the flesh lusteth,* etc. The flesh is said to lust, because the soul does this according to it, as the ear is said to hear, and the eye to see, whereas rather the soul both hears through the ear and sees through the eye. For the flesh lusts nothing save through the soul, but it is said to lust when the soul by carnal concupiscence struggles against the spirit. For the cause of that carnal concupiscence is not in the soul, for it comes to be out of both, because without both no delight is felt.

*But if you are led by the Spirit,* etc. From which it appears that he has not the Holy Spirit who is under the law, not by dispensation, but truly. *You are not under the law.* You have now this advantage, therefore this part is to be chosen. He says that those are damnably under the law whom the law makes guilty, not fulfilling the law while, not knowing grace, they presume upon themselves. Further, he is under the law who abstains from evil by fear, not by love, guilty in will. This law strikes fear, not love.
*The kingdom not of God shall they obtain.* There is no middle place, so that he should not be in punishment who will not be in the kingdom.

*Charity.* He has set the head first, whence the members follow. For no one rejoices well who does not love the good whence he rejoices. He has not true peace with anyone unless he love him. He is not long-suffering in waiting perseveringly unless he be fervent in loving. He is not kind unless he love him whom he helps. He is not good save by loving. He is not faithful healthfully, save by that faith which works through love. He is not meek who is not governed by love. No one holds himself back from that whereby he is defiled unless he love that whereby he is honoured. With reason therefore he so often commends charity, as though it alone were to be enjoined, which cannot be had without the rest by which a man is made good. *Joy.* Purity of conscience. Whence: *There is no rejoicing for the wicked, saith the Lord ((Isa. XLVIII))* .

*But they who.* As if he should say: Against the evil the law is set; but for the good the cross is set. Which he says thus: *But they who,* etc., *have crucified their flesh,* etc. It befits our devotion that we who celebrate the passion of the crucified Lord should make for ourselves a cross of carnal pleasures to be repressed. On this cross indeed ought always in this life to hang the Christian, that he may be fixed with nails and with the precepts of justice, as Christ was fastened with nails on the cross.

*If we live by the spirit.* What he said above in general he turns back upon those to whom he writes, and numbers himself with them, showing by this that he does not say to them what he himself would not be willing to keep. As if he should say: I do not say to you anything which I myself also am unwilling to do.

notes.text: The days are fulfilled that he should be received up — That is, the time of his passion was now at hand. St. Luke looks through this, to the glory which was to follow. He steadfastly set his face - Without fear of his enemies, or shame of the cross, Heb. xii, 2.
He sent messengers to make ready — A lodging and needful entertainment for him and those with him.
His face was as though he would go to Jerusalem — It plainly appeared, he was going to worship at the temple, and thereby, in effect, to condemn the Samaritan worship at Mount Gerizim.

As Elisha did — At or near this very place, which might put it into the minds of the apostles to make the motion now, rather than at any other time or place, where Christ had received the like affront.
Ye know not what manner of spirit — The spirit of Christianity is. It is not a spirit of wrath and vengeance, but of peace, and gentleness, and love.
Matt. viii, 19.
But Jesus said to him — First understand the terms: consider on what conditions thou art to follow me.
Suffer me first to bid them farewell that are in my house — As Elisha did after Elijah had called him from the plough, 1 Kings xix, 19; to which our Lord's answer seems to allude.
Is fit for the kingdom of God — Either to propagate or to receive it.

glossa.text:
*Lord, wilt thou. ((BED.))* The apostles, still rude and ignorant of the measure of vengeance, etc., *as far as* such a power has been conferred by God upon holy men.

*We say that fire come down from heaven.* At the word of these men fire would come down from heaven, because they are the sons of thunder. *And consume them? And turning he rebuked them and said.* In the likeness of Elias, who both by his own hand and by fire divinely obtained put the elders of Baal to death. And in this, that the apostles presume to themselves the power of such a prophet, it is shown that the merit of the prophets was in them.

((AMBR.)) The apostles do not sin, who follow the law, etc., *as far as* he does not seek vengeance who does not fear.
*You know not of what spirit you are.* By whose spirit you have been sealed, whose deeds you imitate, now taking counsel mercifully, but in the future judging justly.

*The Son of man came not to destroy souls, but to save,* etc. Perfect virtue has no zeal for vengeance, nor is there any anger where there is the fulness of charity.

((BED.)) Vengeance is not always to be taken upon those who sin, etc., *as far as* from whom in this place the fire is kept back.
*A certain man said. ((ID.))* This man, moved by the greatness of the signs, wishes to follow, etc., *as far as* and he feigned the service of a disciple, which feigning is figured by the fox.

*The foxes have holes. ((ID.))* The fox is a deceitful animal, intent upon ambushes, practising the robberies of fraud, dwelling in holes even amid the very lodgings of men: so the heretic, not having the house of faith, draws others into his own fraud and seduces them from the faith.

*And he said to another.* Note that the Lord spurned not faults but frauds, because he who rejected the fraudulent man chose the innocent one; but him whose father he knew to be dead, that father of whom it is said: *Forget thy father's house ((Psal. XLIV))*, etc.
*Suffer that the dead. ((BED.))* Mystically. The son is not called back from his duty to his father, etc., *as far as* he ought not to bury the devil's treacheries in himself.

*To take leave of those.* If a disciple about to follow God is rebuked because he wishes to take leave of his house, what will become of those who often, with no profit, visits the houses of their own people which they had forsaken.

echoes.text: I am Yahweh your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, that you should not be their slaves. I have broken the bars of your yoke, and made you go upright.
echoes.note: Paul's 'yoke of bondage/slavery' inverts the exodus formula where God 'broke the bars of your yoke' and made Israel walk upright after Egyptian slavery. Volume is fair (the yoke-of-slavery image is distinctively exodus/covenant) and coheres with Paul's whole exodus-from-law typology in Galatians. The redemptive-liberation logic matches closely.

echoes.text: You shall make the fiftieth year holy, and proclaim liberty throughout the land to all its inhabitants. It shall be a jubilee to you; and each of you shall return to his own property, and each of you shall return to his family.
echoes.note: The Jubilee proclamation of 'liberty (deror) throughout the land' may underlie Paul's stress on the freedom for which Christ liberated. Coherence is real (release from debt-servitude) but volume is faint; the verbal link runs through the LXX language of eleutheria rather than direct citation.

echoes.text: The Spirit of the Lord Yahweh is on me; because Yahweh has anointed me to preach good news to the humble. He has sent me to bind up the broken hearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and release to those who are bound;
echoes.note: The Servant's anointing 'to proclaim liberty to the captives' is a Second-Temple touchstone for eschatological release that Paul's freedom language may draw upon. Faint volume and no verbal quotation, but the messianic-liberty theme coheres with Christ as the agent who 'made us free.'
echoes.lxxText: The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to preach glad tidings to the poor, to heal the broken in heart, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and recovery of sight to the blind;

echoes.text: Thus speaks Yahweh of Armies, the God of Israel, saying, I have broken the yoke of the king of Babylon.
echoes.note: Jeremiah's sign-act of the broken/iron yoke (chs. 27-28) gives the prophetic vocabulary of a yoke as imposed servitude that is broken or re-imposed. Coherence is moderate but recurrence is weak; the image is generic enough that direct dependence is uncertain.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Elijah answered to the captain of fifty, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from the sky, and consume you and your fifty!” Fire came down from the sky, and consumed him and his fifty. Again he sent to him another captain of fifty and his fifty. He answered him, “Man of God, the king has said, ‘Come down quickly!’” Elijah answered them, “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from the sky, and consume you and your fifty!” The fire of God came down […]
echoes.note: 'Command fire to come down from the sky... just as Elijah did' explicitly cites Elijah calling down fire on the messengers from Samaria; the Samaritan setting makes the reference exact. High volume (named comparison) and coherence; Jesus' rebuke signals a deliberate contrast with the Elijah model.

echoes.text: When Yahweh was about to take Elijah up by a whirlwind into heaven, Elijah went with Elisha from Gilgal.
echoes.note: 'The days were near that he should be taken up' and Jesus 'set his face' draw on Elijah's assumption ('when the LORD was about to take up Elijah') and prophetic resolve. The analepsis/analambano language tightly binds the journey's start to Elijah's ascent; high coherence.

echoes.text: For the Lord Yahweh will help me; therefore I have not been confounded: therefore have I set my face like a flint, and I know that I shall not be disappointed.
echoes.note: Jesus 'set his face' resolutely toward Jerusalem echoes the Servant's 'I have set my face like a flint' in obedient suffering. Moderate volume via the face-setting idiom; coherent with the Isaianic Servant strand running through the chapter.

echoes.text: Son of man, set your face toward Jerusalem, and preach toward the sanctuaries, and prophesy against the land of Israel;
echoes.note: 'Set your face toward Jerusalem and prophesy' is a recurring prophetic commission idiom that colors Jesus' face-setting as prophetic confrontation. The phrase is multiply attested in Ezekiel, so diffuse and contested.

echoes.text: So he departed there, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing, with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth: and Elijah passed over to him, and cast his mantle on him. He left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?” He returned from following him, and took the yoke of oxen, and killed them, […]
echoes.note: 'No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back' directly engages Elisha's call: found plowing, he asks to kiss his parents farewell before following, and Elijah lets him. Jesus radicalizes the precedent—no looking back, no delayed farewell—making the plowing image and the farewell request unmistakable. Very high volume and coherence.

echoes.text: He left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?”
echoes.note: 'Allow me first to say good-bye to those at my house' nearly quotes Elisha's 'let me kiss my father and mother, and then I will follow you.' The verbal correspondence in the third would-be follower is the strongest single anchor for the Elisha typology here.

echoes.text: It came to pass, when they had taken them out, that he said, “Escape for your life! Don’t look behind you, and don’t stay anywhere in the plain. Escape to the mountains, lest you be consumed!”
echoes.note: 'Looking back' as fatal hesitation may glance at Lot's wife, the proverbial backward look that forfeits deliverance. Faint and figural relative to the dominant Elisha frame; contested.

echoes.text: And he called him, and said, “My child, if I die, bury me. Don’t despise your mother. Honor her all the days of your life, and do that which is pleasing to her, and don’t grieve her.
echoes.note: 'Let me first bury my father' reflects the supreme filial duty of burial dramatized in Tobit, against which Jesus' 'leave the dead to bury their dead' is shockingly subversive. Deuterocanonical availability illuminates the cultural weight Jesus overturns, though it is background rather than a textual echo.

echoes.text: but the dove found no place to rest her foot, and she returned to him into the ship, for the waters were on the surface of the whole earth. He put out his hand, and took her, and brought her to him into the ship.
echoes.note: 'The birds of the sky have nests, but the Son of Man has no place to lay his head' may faintly invert creation's provision of resting places (the dove finding no rest, then nesting). Very low volume; offered only as a faint figural counterpoint.

registers.label: Spare
lines: Jesus set his face toward Jerusalem, and he calls us to the road.
We will follow you, wherever you go.
No looking back now, no hand lifted from the plow.
Lead us, and we will not turn aside.
Your way was through the sea, your path through the mighty waters.
Yet you led your people like a flock.
Come, take up the journey and worship.
We set out after Jesus. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Elisha watched the mantle fall from the sky, picked it up off the ground, and turned back to the river — the road was his now.
Lead us, and we will follow.
Jesus set his face toward Jerusalem, steady as flint, and the way was long and the cost was real, and still he walked it.
Lead us, and we will follow.
He says, leave the dead to bury the dead, put your hand to the plow and don't look back — the kingdom is up ahead.
Lead us, and we will follow.
Your way once cut a path straight through the sea; you have never lost your people on the road. So we set out. Walk with us.
Lead us, and we will follow. Amen.
